title: What is the replication factor in Kafka, and what are its use cases?
shortTitle: The replication factor in Kafka and its use cases

s1_definition.profdef: The replication factor is a per-topic setting that specifies how many copies of each partition Kafka maintains across different brokers. A replication factor of N means every partition has N identical replicas on N separate brokers — one leader and N minus one followers. The replication factor determines how many broker failures the topic can tolerate without losing data or availability, and it is the primary lever for durability and high availability in Kafka.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India decides how many backup copies of each ledger drawer to keep. A replication factor of three means every drawer is copied into three different branch vaults. If one vault is destroyed in a fire, two identical copies remain, so no records are lost and the bank keeps running. Choosing the number of copies is the replication factor — more copies means more safety, but also more storage and more work keeping them identical.
s1_definition.oneliner: The replication factor is how many copies of each partition Kafka keeps across brokers, and it controls how many failures the topic can survive.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The replication factor is a per-topic setting that specifies how many copies of each partition Kafka maintains across different brokers. A replication factor of N means every partition has N identical replicas on N separate brokers — one leader and N minus one followers. The replication factor determines how many broker failures the topic can tolerate without losing data or availability, and it is the primary lever for durability and high availability in Kafka.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India decides how many backup copies of each ledger drawer to keep. A replication factor of three means every drawer is copied into three different branch vaults. If one vault is destroyed in a fire, two identical copies remain, so no records are lost and the bank keeps running. Choosing the number of copies is the replication factor — more copies means more safety, but also more storage and more work keeping them identical.

**One line to remember:** The replication factor is how many copies of each partition Kafka keeps across brokers, and it controls how many failures the topic can survive.

sections.s2_technical:
You set the replication factor when you create a topic, for example `kafka-topics.sh --create --topic transfers --partitions 6 --replication-factor 3`. Each of the six partitions will then have three replicas spread across three brokers. Kafka places the replicas on different brokers deliberately, so a single broker failure never takes down more than one replica of any partition.

The replication factor directly determines fault tolerance. With a replication factor of N, the topic can tolerate up to N minus one broker failures and still have at least one surviving copy of the data. A replication factor of one means no redundancy — if that broker dies, the partition's data is gone and unavailable. A replication factor of three is the common production standard because it tolerates two broker failures and pairs well with min.insync.replicas of two for strong durability.

The replication factor works together with min.insync.replicas and acks. The replication factor is the total number of copies; min.insync.replicas is how many of those copies must acknowledge a write before it is considered committed when the producer uses acks=all. A typical safe combination is replication factor three and min.insync.replicas two: this guarantees every committed write is on at least two brokers, and you can still accept writes after losing one broker. If you set min.insync.replicas equal to the replication factor, you get maximum durability but lose the ability to write when any single broker is down, which hurts availability.

The replication factor is bounded by the number of brokers. You cannot have a replication factor higher than the number of brokers in the cluster, because each replica must sit on a distinct broker. So a three-broker cluster supports a maximum replication factor of three. You can increase the replication factor of an existing topic, but it requires a reassignment that copies data to new brokers, which is an operational task, so it is best planned up front.

The main use cases for choosing a replication factor are driven by how critical the data is. Financial and transactional topics — transfers, payments, settlements, audit logs — use replication factor three to guarantee no committed record is lost even during failures and maintenance. High-availability topics that must keep serving during rolling upgrades also use three, because you can take one broker down for patching and still have two copies. Cross-rack or cross-availability-zone durability uses replica placement with a replication factor of three so copies land in different failure domains. By contrast, non-critical, easily regenerated data such as transient metrics or a dev environment might use replication factor one or two to save storage and network cost, accepting that a failure could lose that data.

The senior-level nuance is cost versus safety. Each extra replica multiplies storage and inter-broker network traffic, because every write must be copied to every replica. Replication factor three roughly triples the storage and the replication bandwidth compared to one. So you match the replication factor to the data's importance: three for anything involving money or compliance, and lower only for data you can afford to lose. You also consider rack-awareness configuration so the three replicas are spread across racks or availability zones, protecting against the loss of an entire zone rather than just a single broker.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India must decide the replication factor for each of its Kafka topics based on how critical the data is, and the platform team builds a helper that recommends and validates the setting.

Problem 1 — The transfers and settlements topics carry money movement; losing even one committed record is unacceptable, and the system must survive broker failures and maintenance. This is exactly the case for replication factor three with min.insync.replicas two.

Problem 2 — A metrics topic carries transient dashboard numbers that are regenerated every few seconds; losing some during a failure is harmless and storage cost matters. This is exactly the case for a lower replication factor to save cost.

Problem 3 — A proposed topic requests a replication factor of five, but the cluster has only three brokers. This is exactly the constraint that the replication factor cannot exceed the broker count, which must be rejected.

The mini-project is a replication-factor advisor. We build a `TopicSpec` domain object, a `ReplicationAdvisor` that recommends a replication factor and min.insync.replicas by data criticality, and a `ClusterValidator` that rejects a replication factor larger than the broker count. The demo evaluates a transfers topic, a metrics topic, and an invalid over-replicated topic, logging the recommendation and validation.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the demo
javac com/bank/rfadvisor/demo/RfAdvisorDemo.java
java com.bank.rfadvisor.demo.RfAdvisorDemo

# Create a critical topic with replication factor 3
kafka-topics.sh --create --topic transfers --partitions 6 \
  --replication-factor 3 --bootstrap-server kafka1:9092
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is three topic requests: transfers (critical), dashboard-metrics (transient), and over-replicated (invalid, requesting five copies on three brokers).

Step 1 — The advisor evaluates transfers with criticality CRITICAL. It returns a TopicSpec with replication factor three and min.insync.replicas two, explaining that money movement needs no committed loss and must survive one broker going down. This spec lives in memory.

Step 2 — The validator checks the transfers spec against the three-broker cluster. Replication factor three is not greater than three brokers, and min.insync two is not greater than the replication factor, so the spec is valid.

Step 3 — The advisor evaluates dashboard-metrics with criticality TRANSIENT. It returns replication factor one and min.insync one, explaining that regenerable data uses a low factor to save storage and replication bandwidth.

Step 4 — The validator checks the metrics spec. Replication factor one is valid on a three-broker cluster, so it passes.

Step 5 — The over-replicated request asks for replication factor five on a three-broker cluster. The validator detects that five exceeds the broker count of three and rejects it as invalid. The logs show two valid recommendations tuned to data criticality and one correctly rejected request, demonstrating how the replication factor is chosen and bounded.

```
2026-10-24 20:30:00 [INFO] transfers -> RF=3 minInSync=2 : money movement: RF=3, min.insync=2, acks=all — no committed loss, survive 1 broker down
2026-10-24 20:30:00 [INFO] VALID transfers RF=3
2026-10-24 20:30:00 [INFO] dashboard-metrics -> RF=1 minInSync=1 : regenerable data: RF=1 to save storage and replication bandwidth
2026-10-24 20:30:00 [INFO] VALID dashboard-metrics RF=1
2026-10-24 20:30:00 [WARNING] over-replicated requested RF=5 on a 3-broker cluster
2026-10-24 20:30:00 [SEVERE] INVALID over-replicated: RF=5 exceeds broker count 3
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Topic request (name + criticality)
    │
    ▼
  ReplicationAdvisor.recommend(criticality)
    │
    ├─ CRITICAL  → RF=3, minInSync=2  (transfers, settlements)
    ├─ IMPORTANT → RF=3, minInSync=2  (HA during upgrades)
    └─ TRANSIENT → RF=1, minInSync=1  (metrics, dev)
    │
    ▼
  ClusterValidator.validate(spec)   [brokerCount = 3]
    │
    ├─ RF > brokerCount? ──yes──→ REJECT (cannot place replicas)
    ├─ minInSync > RF? ──yes──→ REJECT (impossible to satisfy)
    └─ else ──→ ACCEPT

  Example placement RF=3 on partition P0:
    broker-1 [leader] ── copy ──→ broker-2 [follower] ── copy ──→ broker-3 [follower]
    tolerate up to RF-1 = 2 broker failures
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The replication factor is a per-topic setting that says how many copies of each partition Kafka keeps across different brokers. A replication factor of three means every partition has three identical replicas on three separate brokers — one leader and two followers. It is the primary lever for durability and high availability, because it determines how many broker failures the topic can survive: a replication factor of N tolerates up to N minus one broker failures and still has a surviving copy.

The replication factor works together with min.insync.replicas and the producer acks setting. The replication factor is the total number of copies, while min.insync.replicas is how many of those copies must acknowledge a write, under acks=all, before it is committed. The standard safe combination is replication factor three with min.insync.replicas two, which guarantees every committed write lives on at least two brokers and still lets you accept writes after losing one broker. One important constraint is that the replication factor can never exceed the number of brokers, because each replica must sit on a distinct broker.

The use cases come down to how critical the data is. For financial and transactional topics — transfers, payments, settlements, audit logs — I use replication factor three so no committed record is ever lost and the system keeps serving during broker failures and rolling maintenance. For transient, easily regenerated data like dashboard metrics, a lower replication factor saves storage and replication bandwidth. I also use rack-aware placement so the three replicas land in different availability zones, protecting against the loss of an entire zone.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, every money-movement topic runs at replication factor three with min.insync.replicas two, while non-critical telemetry runs lower to control cost. The senior point I always make is that this is a cost-versus-safety decision: each extra replica roughly multiplies storage and inter-broker network traffic, so I match the replication factor to the importance of the data — three for anything touching money or compliance, and lower only for data I can afford to lose.

keyPoints: Replication factor: copies of each partition across brokers
ISR (In-Sync Replicas): followers caught up with leader
acks=all: wait for all ISR to acknowledge — strongest durability
